content:
According to reports, the source code of the camera app in the latest iOS 27 beta shows that several important professional photography and video recording features are about to be added.

Although the built-in camera app has gradually added new features over time, for an app mainly designed for point-and-shoot photography, this discovery is still surprising...

Apple has always tried to strike a balance between the two — on one hand, making its own camera app extremely easy to use for ordinary users, while on the other hand providing a certain degree of creative control for users who take photography seriously. However, despite years of evolution, most serious photographers and videographers still prefer to use third-party apps.

If these findings are true, some powerful features usually associated with professional cameras are about to be added, which could change the status quo. Developer pdfu says they found source code supporting four major features, all of which are disabled in the beta stage.

Exposure monitoring tools

Relying solely on the naked eye to judge exposure is prone to errors, especially when looking at the iPhone screen under harsh sunlight. Most professional cameras support a histogram function that accurately reflects exposure status; video editing software typically uses a waveform monitor to display similar information. pdfu says they found source code for these two features in the beta.

Focus peaking display

The depth of field range from near to far in a photo is affected by many factors, but in certain scenes only part of the range is sharp. Similarly, relying solely on the naked eye to judge which areas are in focus and which are not is extremely unreliable, so professional cameras commonly use a method called focus peaking display.

Once this feature is enabled, a marker overlay effect can be turned on to highlight the in-focus parts of the image — usually in red, although the example on the left uses yellow.

Highlight overexposure warning

The biggest risk of exposure errors is overexposure. Generally speaking, if shadows are underexposed, they can usually be corrected in post-production — unless it is so severe that the dark areas are completely black (RGB value of zero). Overexposure is much more troublesome, because highlights can easily be completely blown out, meaning the bright parts exceed RGB 255, which cannot be recovered in post-production.

Many professional cameras use what is called zebra stripes, using red diagonal lines to mark areas that are completely blown out. Some cameras can even let users manually set this threshold, so you receive a warning when approaching overexposure (for example, reaching 90%), rather than only knowing when it is actually blown out.

This feature is also shown on the right side of the image above.

Manual focus

Although the current camera app can lock the focus position of the subject in the frame via AE/AF lock (auto exposure / auto focus), it can only lock exposure and focus at the same point simultaneously.

Reports say Apple has been testing adding a slider in the camera app to achieve true manual focus. pdfu says this feature may be limited to one or more upcoming new iPhone models.

Other features

In addition to professional features, it is reported that an option for a countdown timer burst selfie mode will also be added. When taking group photos, many people always want to take a few more shots; this feature allows the iPhone to be placed on a tripod or fixed in a certain position, then continuously take multiple photos, and pick one that everyone is satisfied with.

Finally, there are indications that a new image processing method will be adopted, to match the variable aperture expected to appear on the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac's view

The above features have not been enabled in any iOS 27 beta, and I am surprised that Apple would put them in the built-in camera app rather than restricting them to Final Cut Camera, but this report appears credible.

What are your thoughts on this report? Feel free to share your opinions in the comment area.
